title: Personal Financial Literacy Exam
blurb: Practice questions for the Personal Financial Literacy exam, reused from public-domain U.S. government sources: the SEC's Investor.gov investing quizzes and the FDIC's Money Smart for Adults answer keys.
disclaimer: Questions reused from openly licensed sources (credited on each question). Not official DECA exam content.
coverageNote: Areas follow the DECA Personal Financial Literacy blueprint (Earning Income, Spending, Saving, Investing, Managing Credit, Managing Risk). The open sources lean heavily on investing and fraud, so Earning Income (2), Spending (5) and Managing Credit (9) are thin, and insurance has 1 item. No source item was written or reworded to fill those gaps. Investor.gov quiz items keep their wording; their "Q1."-style question numbers were dropped for display, which is not counted as an adaptation.

questions.stem: What is a 401(k) plan?
choices: Retirement savings plan sponsored by an employer
questions.explanation: A 401(k) plan is an employer-sponsored retirement savings plan that gives employees a choice of investment options. Employer-sponsored retirement plans generally fall into two categories: defined contribution plans and defined benefit plans. A defined contribution plan, such as a 401(k) plan, does not promise you a specific payment upon retirement. In these plans, you or your employer (or both) contribute to your individual account under the plan. A defined benefit plan promises you a specified monthly benefit at retirement. The benefit may be a fixed dollar amount or may depend on a plan formula that considers factors such as salary and years of service.

questions.stem: The strategy of setting up regular automatic deductions from your paycheck or bank account into a savings or investment account to keep yourself on track toward your short and long-term financial goals is known as:
choices: Putting all of your eggs in one basket
questions.explanation: Many people get into the habit of saving and investing by following this advice: always pay yourself or your family first. They find it easier to pay themselves first if they allow their bank to automatically remove money from their paycheck and deposit it into a savings or investment account.

choices: Creating a saving and investing plan
questions.explanation: Create and stick to a budget that considers your monthly expenses, including necessities like living expenses and discretionary expenses like entertainment. It is important to keep your “needs” versus “wants” in check and strive to live within your means.

questions.stem: Aidan started an investment account. If the account earns an average investment return of 7%, Aidan’s initial investment will double in approximately
choices: 14 years, assuming additional contributions of 10% of the principal
20 years, assuming additional contributions of 10% of the principal
questions.explanation: The Rule of 72 is a great way to estimate how an investment will grow over time. If you know the rate of return, the Rule of 72 can tell you approximately how long it will take for the investment to double in value. Simply divide the number 72 by the investment’s expected rate of return. Assuming an expected rate of return of 7%, an investment, assuming no additional contributions, will double in value about every 10 years (72 divided by 7 equals 10.3).

questions.stem: An emergency fund can help pay for which of the following unexpected expenses?
questions.explanation: Saving three to six months of living expenses in an emergency fund will provide you with peace of mind when life throws unexpected financial emergencies at you. Whether it is a car accident, medical issue, or other unexpected repair or expense, having an emergency fund can help you weather these financial situations and minimize the impact they may have on your future financial and investing plans.

questions.stem: A federally insured savings account with which of the following annual interest rates will grow most quickly?
questions.explanation: Generally speaking, an account with the highest annual interest rate will grow the fastest. Among accounts with the same annual interest rate, the account earning interest that compounds the most frequently will grow the fastest.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of using a 529 education savings plan to save for educational expenses:
choices: unlimited investment option changes each year
guaranteed admission at in-state colleges and universities
tax-free earnings that grow over a period of time
questions.explanation: One of the benefits of 529 plans is the tax-free earnings that grow over a period of time. The longer your money is invested, the more time it has to grow and the greater your tax benefits. You will lose some of these potential benefits if you withdraw money from a 529 plan account within a short period of time after it is contributed.

questions.stem: Why is starting to invest as early as possible such a powerful advantage for financial independence?
choices: You get better at picking stocks
You get the benefit of compound growth
You get more access to credit
questions.explanation: Your first step to financial independence is to create a plan that meets your financial goals. Think about what is important to you as you make your plan. questions.explanation: The Rule of 72 is a great way to estimate how an investment will grow over time. questions.stem: Which investment will have the highest value after three years?
choices: Investment A: Year 1 return = +40%, Year 2 return = +0%, Year 3 return = -10%
Investment B: Year 1 return = -10%, Year 2 return = +0%, Year 3 return = +40%
Investment C: Year 1 return = +10%, Year 2 return = +10%, Year 3 return = +10%
Each will have the same value after three years
questions.explanation: Investment A and Investment B will have the same value, but that value will be lower than Investment C. Let’s assume an initial balance of $10,000 for each investment. If the rate of return for Investment A in Year 1 is 40%, then the value of Investment A will be $14,000 after Year 1. It will also be $14,000 after Year 2 if the rate of return is zero percent for that year. If the rate of return for Investment A in Year 3 is -10%, then the value of the Investment A will be $12,600 after Year 3. If the rate of return for Investment B in Year 1 is -10%, then the value of the Investment B will be $9,000 after Year 1. It will also be $9,000 after Year 2 if the rate of return is zero percent for that year. If the rate of return for Investment B in Year 3 is 40%, then the value of the Investment B will be $12,600 after Year 3. If the rate of return for Investment C in Year 1 is 10%, then the value of the Investment C will be 11,000 after Year 1. If the rate of return for Investment C in Year 2 is (again) 10%, then the value of the Investment A will be 12,100 after Year 2. If the rate of return for Investment C in Year 3 is (yet again) 10%, then the value of Investment C will be $13,310.

questions.stem: Champ owes $2,000 on a loan and the interest rate on the loan is 24% per year compounded annually. If Champ didn’t pay anything off, at this interest rate, how many years would it take for the amount to double to $4,000?
questions.explanation: Compound interest can work for you when you save and invest, but it can also work against you if you have taken out a loan! The Rule of 72 can tell you approximately how long it will take for the principal of a loan to double in value (assuming no payments toward the loan are made). Simply divide the number 72 by the interest rate. A loan with an interest rate of 24% will double in value about every 3 years (72 divided by 24 equals 3).

questions.stem: A Ponzi scheme is an investment fraud that pays existing investors with funds collected from new investors. Which of the following is a Ponzi scheme “red flag”?
choices: High returns with little or no risk
questions.explanation: A Ponzi scheme is an investment fraud that pays existing investors with funds collected from new investors. Ponzi scheme organizers often promise to invest your money and generate high returns with little or no risk. But in many Ponzi schemes, the fraudsters do not invest the money. Instead, they use it to pay those who invested earlier and may keep some for themselves. Many Ponzi schemes share common characteristics. Look for these warning signs: high returns with little or no risk; overly consistent returns; unregistered investments; unlicensed sellers; secretive, complex strategies; issues with paperwork; and difficulty receiving payments.

choices: They often hide their true identities

questions.explanation: In a relationship investment scam, fraudsters — including criminals and other bad actors — often hide their true identities, reach out to unsuspecting targets (often online or through text messages), gain their trust over time, and then defraud them through fake investments. Relationship investment scams are sometimes referred to by various terms including romance scams, “cryptocurrency” investment scams, financial grooming scams, and even the distasteful term “pig butchering scams.” These scams also sometimes involve “catfishing,” where fraudsters might set up fake online identities to carry out crimes.

questions.stem: It is never a good idea to invest money based on:
choices: Advice solely from someone you met online
Promises of high returns with little or no risk
questions.explanation: Do not invest money based on advice from someone you have solely met online or through an app. Do not share with them any information relating to your personal finances or identity. Do not make investment decisions based solely on advice from someone famous. Be skeptical and ask yourself: “Why is this person endorsing this investment, and does it fit in my financial plan?” Do not trust someone who pressures you to invest right away or promises big returns with little or no risk. There is no such thing as high guaranteed returns, and every investment involves risk. If an offer sounds too good to be true, it probably is.
